## formal
Work in $\Cl(1,3)$ with $\gamma_{0}^{2} = 1$, $\gamma_{1}^{2} = \gamma_{2}^{2} = \gamma_{3}^{2} = -1$, $I_{4} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$, $\sigma_{j} = \gamma_{j}\gamma_{0}$, $I\sigma_{3} = I_{4}\sigma_{3}$; spinors are even multivectors and the field theory's unit is $I_{4}$ (on spinors $L_{I_{4}} = R_{I_{4}}$, $L_{a}\psi = a\psi$, $R_{b}\psi = \psi b$). For future null $k = \omega(\gamma_{0} + n)$ ($\omega > 0$, $n \cdot \gamma_{0} = 0$, $Q(n) = -1$) put $B_{k} = \gamma_{0}n$, $D_{k} = I_{4}B_{k}$ (for $k = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1}$, the wedge boost $\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}$ and the dual plane $\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$ of \claimref{synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-the-two-pi-rotor-so-geometric-modular-conjugations-give-interacting-spin-statistics}), $S_{k} = \{\psi \in \Cl^{+}(1,3) : k\psi = 0\}$, and call $\psi(x) = e^{-sI_{4}k\cdot x}\psi_{0}$, $\psi_{0} \in S_{k}$, $s = \pm 1$, a massless mode of frequency sign $s$. Let $\Gamma\psi = I_{4}\psi I\sigma_{3}$ be the chirality (the projectors $\chi_{e} = \tfrac12(1 - e\Gamma)$ of \claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Helicity locked to the frequency sign; proved.)} $\dim S_{k} = 4$, $L_{B_{k}} = -1$ and $L_{D_{k}} = -L_{I_{4}}$ on $S_{k}$. The rotation by $\theta$ about $n$, right-handed for $I_{3} = \gamma_{0}I_{4}$, is $\exp(\tfrac{\theta}{2}D_{k})$ and acts on $S_{k}$ as $e^{-I_{4}\theta/2}$; so a mode of frequency sign $s$ has energy $s\omega$, momentum direction $sn$ and helicity $s/2$ relative to $I_{4}$, for either chirality.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The unit and the chirality; proved.)} $\Gamma^{2} = 1$ and $L_{I_{4}} = -\Gamma R_{I\sigma_{3}}$ on $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$; $\Gamma$ commutes with the left rotor action and preserves $S_{k}$, with $2$-dimensional eigenspaces there. On a mode of chirality $\gamma$ the charge rotation $R_{I\sigma_{3}}$ equals $-\gamma L_{I_{4}}$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Covariant maps are $I_{4}$-linear; proved.)} Every real-linear map of $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$ commuting with left multiplication by the Lorentz rotors is a right multiplication $R_{c}$, $c \in \Cl^{+}(1,3)$; hence it commutes with $L_{I_{4}}$ and preserves the frequency sign of every mode.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Discrete maps; proved for the stated family.)} Let $\psi(x) \mapsto a\psi(\Lambda^{-1}x)b$, $a, b$ basis blades of the same parity, $\Lambda \in \{1, P, T, PT\}$ acting on vectors as $x$, $\gamma_{0}x\gamma_{0}$, $-\gamma_{0}x\gamma_{0}$, $-x$. It carries modes to modes with $s' = s(-1)^{|a|}\sgn(\gamma_{0}\cdot\Lambda k)$ and chirality $\gamma' = (-1)^{|a|}c(b)\gamma$, $c(b) = \pm 1$ as $b$ commutes or anticommutes with $I\sigma_{3}$. It keeps the massless equation exactly when $a \in \pm\{1, I_{4}\}$ for $\Lambda = 1, PT$ and $a \in \pm\{\gamma_{0}, \gamma_{0}I_{4}\}$ for $\Lambda = P, T$; within this family the frequency sign relative to $I_{4}$ flips exactly for $\Lambda \in \{P, PT\}$, the maps reversing the spatial orientation $I_{3}$. The charge conjugation $\psi \mapsto \psi\sigma_{1}$ flips the chirality and not the frequency sign; the CP map $\psi(x) \mapsto \gamma_{0}\psi(Px)\gamma_{0}\sigma_{1}$ flips the frequency sign and not the chirality; every pair $(s, \gamma)$ occurs on every $S_{k}$.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Consequence; argued.)} The orientation datum of Premise \claimref{synthesis.n-plus-null-ground-state}, null vacuum versus filled sea relative to $I_{4}$ and the time orientation, is on massless modes the frequency sign relative to $I_{4}$: it is odd under spatial-orientation reversal and under CP, and even under charge conjugation, while the chirality of the doublets is odd under charge conjugation and even under CP. So the datum is not the chirality of the doublets; by (i) it can be read as a helicity orientation.
\end{enumerate}
Transport-absent.

## technical
The premise (N$_{+}$) leaves one orientation open: which of the two states with the same local data, the null vacuum or the filled sea, is the state of the light rays, a sign fixed only relative to the field unit $I_{4}$ and the direction of time. One might hope this sign is the handedness that the weak doublets already carry. For massless even spinors it is not. On the kernel of a null momentum the boost bivector acts as $-1$, so the rotation bivector of the dual plane acts as $-I_{4}$; every massless mode then has helicity equal to half its frequency sign relative to $I_{4}$, whatever its chirality (the sampled helicity statement of \claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}, now proved for every direction). The field unit is minus the chirality times the charge rotation, $L_{I_{4}} = -\Gamma R_{I\sigma_{3}}$. The maps of spinors commuting with the Lorentz rotors are right multiplications, so they commute with $I_{4}$ and never change a frequency sign. Among the discrete maps $a\psi(\Lambda^{-1}x)b$ that keep the massless equation (classified here: $a$ is $1$ or $I_{4}$ for the identity and $PT$, $\gamma_{0}$ or $\gamma_{0}I_{4}$ for $P$ and $T$), the frequency sign flips exactly when the spatial orientation is reversed, while the chirality flips according to the parities of $a$ and $b$. Charge conjugation $\psi \mapsto \psi\sigma_{1}$ flips the chirality alone, CP flips the frequency sign alone. So the (N$_{+}$) datum and the chirality are independent bits; the identification fails its pre-registered kill condition. The consequence for the premise, that the datum is not the doublets' chirality, is argued from these transformation rules. The identity $I_{4}B = D$ of \claimref{synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-the-two-pi-rotor-so-geometric-modular-conjugations-give-interacting-spin-statistics} is re-derived, not used, so the result rests on no premise. Transport-absent.

## lay
The series assumes that the quantum modes on a horizon are in their lowest-energy state, but which of two mirror-image states that is depends on an orientation: how the field's imaginary unit, here the four-dimensional volume element of spacetime, is oriented relative to the direction of time. A natural guess is that this orientation is the same thing as the left-handedness of the particles the weak force acts on. For massless particles it is not. The orientation fixes the spin of each massless wave along its direction of motion, for left- and right-handed particles alike. Exchanging particles and antiparticles changes handedness without changing the orientation, and combining that with a mirror reflection changes the orientation without changing handedness, so the two cannot be one bit.

## one-liner
For massless even spinors with the field unit $I_{4}$, the frequency sign fixes the helicity, $\lambda = s/2$, for either chirality; pointwise Lorentz-covariant maps are right multiplications and keep it; among the discrete maps $a\psi(\Lambda^{-1}x)b$ keeping the massless equation it flips exactly under $P$ and $PT$, and charge conjugation $\psi\sigma_{1}$ flips the chirality alone while CP flips the frequency sign alone, so the orientation datum of (N$_{+}$) is not the doublets' chirality (argued).

proofs.proof-main.tex:
\emph{Notation.} $\Cl(1,3)$ with $\gamma_{0}^{2} = 1$, $\gamma_{j}^{2} = -1$ ($j = 1, 2, 3$), $I_{4} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$, $I_{3} = \gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3} = \gamma_{0}I_{4}$, $\sigma_{j} = \gamma_{j}\gamma_{0}$, $I\sigma_{3} = I_{4}\sigma_{3} = \gamma_{2}\gamma_{1}$. Spinors are elements of $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$; $L_{a}\psi = a\psi$, $R_{b}\psi = \psi b$. $I_{4}$ commutes with every even element and anticommutes with every vector, so on spinors $L_{I_{4}} = R_{I_{4}}$, and $R_{b}$ commutes with every $L_{a}$. Two basis blades either commute or anticommute.

\emph{Step 1 (the null kernel; (i)).} Let $k = \omega(\gamma_{0} + n)$, $\omega > 0$, $n \cdot \gamma_{0} = 0$, $Q(n) = -1$, and $B_{k} = \gamma_{0}n$. Then $k = \omega\gamma_{0}(1 + B_{k})$ and $B_{k}^{2} = -\gamma_{0}^{2}n^{2} = 1$, so $k\psi = 0$ if and only if $B_{k}\psi = -\psi$: $S_{k}$ is the $-1$ eigenspace of the involution $L_{B_{k}}$ on $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$. For a unit transverse $t$ ($t \cdot \gamma_{0} = t \cdot n = 0$, $Q(t) = -1$) the even element $u = \gamma_{0}t$ anticommutes with $B_{k}$, so $L_{u}$ exchanges the two eigenspaces and $\dim S_{k} = 4$. With $D_{k} = I_{4}B_{k}$ and $\psi \in S_{k}$, $D_{k}\psi = I_{4}B_{k}\psi = -I_{4}\psi$, so $L_{D_{k}} = -L_{I_{4}}$ on $S_{k}$. For $k = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1}$, $B_{k} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}$ and $D_{k} = \gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$: the wedge boost and dual plane of \claimref{synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-the-two-pi-rotor-so-geometric-modular-conjugations-give-interacting-spin-statistics}, whose identity $I_{4}B = D$ is the one-line computation above (re-derived here, not taken as a premise). The argument holds for every $n$ at once; equivalently, a rotor $R$ fixing $\gamma_{0}$ carries $\gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1}$ to every future null direction, and $(RkR^{-1})(R\psi) = Rk\psi$ shows $RS_{k} = S_{RkR^{-1}}$, so the case $k = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1}$ suffices.

The plane $D_{k}$ is orthogonal to $\gamma_{0}$ and $n$, and $R_{\theta} = \exp(\tfrac{\theta}{2}D_{k})$ is the rotation by $\theta$ about $n$, right-handed for the spatial orientation $I_{3} = \gamma_{0}I_{4}$ (for $n = \gamma_{1}$: $R_{\theta}\gamma_{2}R_{\theta}^{-1} = \gamma_{2}e^{-\theta\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}} = \cos\theta\,\gamma_{2} + \sin\theta\,\gamma_{3}$). On $S_{k}$, $R_{\theta}\psi = (\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2} - \sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,I_{4})\psi = e^{-I_{4}\theta/2}\psi$: writing the action of a one-parameter group as $e^{-I_{4}\theta J}$, the spin about $n$ is $J = +\tfrac12$ on all of $S_{k}$. For the mode $\psi(x) = e^{-sI_{4}k\cdot x}\psi_{0}$, $\psi_{0} \in S_{k}$, the translation by $a$ gives $\psi(x - a) = e^{sI_{4}k\cdot a}\psi(x)$, so with $e^{I_{4}a\cdot P}$ the energy-momentum relative to $I_{4}$ is $P = sk$: energy $s\omega$, momentum direction $sn$. The rotation about $sn$ by $\theta$ is the rotation about $n$ by $s\theta$, with generator $sJ$: the helicity relative to $I_{4}$ is $s/2$. This is clause (iii) of \claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes} (helicity $+\tfrac12$ of every massless even spinor at positive frequency), there checked on samples, here proved for every null direction and both frequency signs.

\emph{Step 2 (the chirality; (ii)).} $\Gamma = L_{I_{4}}R_{I\sigma_{3}}$ has $\Gamma^{2} = L_{I_{4}^{2}}R_{(I\sigma_{3})^{2}} = 1$ and $\Gamma R_{I\sigma_{3}} = L_{I_{4}}R_{(I\sigma_{3})^{2}} = -L_{I_{4}}$, which is (ii). $\Gamma$ commutes with $L_{a}$ for even $a$ and anticommutes with $L_{v}$ for vectors $v$; so it commutes with the left rotor action, and $k\Gamma\psi = -\Gamma k\psi$ shows that it preserves $S_{k}$. $R_{\sigma_{1}}$ commutes with $L_{k}$ and anticommutes with $\Gamma$ ($\sigma_{1}$ anticommutes with $I\sigma_{3} = \sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}$), so it exchanges the two eigenspaces of $\Gamma$ on $S_{k}$, each of dimension $2$. The projectors $\chi_{e} = \tfrac12(1 - e\Gamma)$ are those of \claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}, so its label $e$ is $-\Gamma$. On a mode of chirality $\Gamma = \gamma$, (ii) gives $R_{I\sigma_{3}} = -\gamma L_{I_{4}}$: the charge rotation $\psi \mapsto \psi e^{I\sigma_{3}\alpha}$ acts as $e^{-\gamma I_{4}\alpha}$.

\emph{Step 3 (covariant maps; (iii)).} For a bivector blade $B$, $1 + tB$ is a positive multiple of a rotor ($B^{2} = -1$, any real $t$; $B^{2} = 1$, $|t| < 1$), so the linear span of the rotors contains $1$ and every bivector; being closed under products it is $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$, which the bivectors generate. A real-linear $T$ commuting with every left rotor multiplication therefore commutes with every $L_{a}$, $a \in \Cl^{+}(1,3)$, and $T(\psi) = T(L_{\psi}1) = L_{\psi}T(1) = R_{T(1)}\psi$: $T$ is right multiplication by $T(1)$, and it commutes with $L_{I_{4}}$. (In the language of the centre: $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$ is a simple algebra with centre $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$, and the commutant of its left regular action is its right action; the elementary form above needs no structure theory.) Such a map preserves every $S_{k}$ and every frequency sign $s$, since $T(e^{-sI_{4}k\cdot x}\psi_{0}) = e^{-sI_{4}k\cdot x}T(\psi_{0})$.

\emph{Step 4 (the discrete maps; (iv)).} The four maps $\Lambda$ act on vectors by $x$, $\gamma_{0}x\gamma_{0}$, $-\gamma_{0}x\gamma_{0}$, $-x$; each is orthogonal and its own inverse, so $k\cdot\Lambda^{-1}x = (\Lambda k)\cdot x$. For the mode $\psi$ above, $a\psi(\Lambda^{-1}x)b = a\,e^{-sI_{4}(\Lambda k)\cdot x}\psi_{0}b = e^{-s(-1)^{|a|}I_{4}(\Lambda k)\cdot x}\,a\psi_{0}b$, since an odd blade anticommutes with $I_{4}$. If $\Lambda k$ is past, write $k' = -\Lambda k$. So the image is the mode with future $k' = \epsilon\Lambda k$, $\epsilon = \sgn(\gamma_{0}\cdot\Lambda k)$, frequency sign $s' = s(-1)^{|a|}\epsilon$ and amplitude $a\psi_{0}b$; $\epsilon = +1$ for $\Lambda = 1, P$ and $-1$ for $T, PT$.

\emph{Which maps keep the equation.} A mode solves the massless equation exactly when its amplitude lies in the null kernel: $\nabla(e^{-sI_{4}k\cdot x}\psi_{0}) = -sk I_{4}e^{-sI_{4}k\cdot x}\psi_{0} = sI_{4}e^{sI_{4}k\cdot x}k\psi_{0}$. So the map keeps the equation on all modes if and only if $(\Lambda k)a\psi_{0} = 0$ for every future null $k$ and every $\psi_{0} \in S_{k}$ ($b$ is invertible). For $\Lambda = 1, PT$ put $c = a$; for $\Lambda = P, T$, $(\Lambda k)a = \pm\gamma_{0}k(\gamma_{0}a)$, put $c = \gamma_{0}a$; the condition is $kc\psi_{0} = 0$. Write $ckc^{-1} = \tilde k$, the vector $k$ with the signs of its components along the generators that anticommute with $c$ reversed; the condition is $\tilde k\psi_{0} = 0$ on $S_{k}$. If $c \in \{1, I_{4}\}$ (up to sign), $\tilde k = \pm k$ and it holds. Otherwise the grade $r$ of $c$ is $1$, $2$ or $3$, so some generator lies in $c$ and some does not, and these two classes are reversed with opposite signs ($\gamma_{\mu}$ in $c$ is multiplied by $(-1)^{r-1}$, $\gamma_{\mu}$ not in $c$ by $(-1)^{r}$); one class contains $\gamma_{0}$ and the other some $\gamma_{j}$, and for $k = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{j}$, $\tilde k = \pm(\gamma_{0} - \gamma_{j})$, whose kernel is the $+1$ eigenspace of $L_{\gamma_{0}\gamma_{j}}$, while $S_{k}$ is its $-1$ eigenspace (Step 1): $\tilde k\psi_{0} \ne 0$ for $\psi_{0} \ne 0$. So the family is exactly $a \in \pm\{1, I_{4}\}$ for $\Lambda = 1, PT$ and $a \in \pm\{\gamma_{0}, \gamma_{0}I_{4}\}$ ($\gamma_{0}I_{4} = I_{3}$) for $\Lambda = P, T$, with $b$ any blade of the parity of $a$: $16$ maps up to sign for each $\Lambda$. Hence $(-1)^{|a|}\epsilon = +1, -1, +1, -1$ for $\Lambda = 1, P, T, PT$: the frequency sign flips exactly for $P$ and $PT$, whatever $a$ and $b$, that is, exactly for the maps that reverse the spatial orientation $I_{3}$ (both $P$ and $T$ reverse $I_{4}$; $T$ also reverses $\gamma_{0}$, and $I_{3} = \gamma_{0}I_{4}$).

\emph{Chirality, helicity and charge of the image.} $\Gamma(a\psi_{0}b) = I_{4}a\psi_{0}bI\sigma_{3} = (-1)^{|a|}c(b)\,a(\Gamma\psi_{0})b$, where $c(b) = \pm 1$ as $b$ commutes or anticommutes with $I\sigma_{3}$; $\Gamma$ commutes with the phase $e^{-s'I_{4}k'\cdot x}$, so the image of a chirality-$\gamma$ mode has chirality $\gamma' = (-1)^{|a|}c(b)\gamma$. By Step 1 its helicity is $s'/2$, and by Step 2 its charge sign relative to $I_{4}$ is $-\gamma'$. Examples: $a = 1$, $b = \sigma_{1}$, $\Lambda = 1$ (the spacetime-algebra charge conjugation $\psi \mapsto \psi\sigma_{1}$): $s' = s$ and $c(\sigma_{1}) = -1$, so the chirality flips and the frequency sign does not; $a = b = \gamma_{0}$, $\Lambda = P$ (parity): both flip; $a = \gamma_{0}$, $b = \gamma_{0}\sigma_{1} = -\gamma_{1}$, $\Lambda = P$ (their product, a CP map): $s' = -s$ and $\gamma' = (-1)(-1)\gamma = \gamma$, so the frequency sign flips and the chirality does not. With the identity these realise all four patterns, and by Step 2 every pair $(s, \gamma)$ occurs on every $S_{k}$: the two labels are independent.

\emph{Step 5 (the consequence; argued).} The datum of Premise \claimref{synthesis.n-plus-null-ground-state}, which of the null vacuum and the filled sea is the state, is fixed relative to the unit $I_{4}$ and the time orientation, and on massless modes it is the choice of which frequency sign $s$ relative to $I_{4}$ counts as positive energy. By Step 4 this sign is odd under every map of the family that reverses the spatial orientation and under CP, and even under the charge conjugation; the chirality is odd under the charge conjugation and parity and even under CP. A rule identifying the datum with the handedness of the chiral (weak) doublets would equate a bit odd under CP with a bit even under it, so it is invariant under none of these maps; and by (iii) no pointwise Lorentz-covariant map changes $s$ at all. Since the helicity relative to $I_{4}$ is $s/2$ for either chirality (Step 1), the datum can equally be read as a helicity orientation of the massless modes; it is not a chirality. Whether some other structure of the series ties the datum to the doublets is not addressed. The checks verify Steps 1 to 4 exactly on sampled null directions (rotation and boost images of $\gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1}$), the commutant dimension, and the full list of blade pairs.
